content: The analysis of reducing saturated fatty acid (SFA) intake to less than 10% of total energy intake yielded results that were challenging to interpret, with wide confidence intervals for pooled effect estimates. No significant effects on cardiovascular or mortality outcomes were observed when SFA intake was reduced to below 10% of total energy intake. A meta-analysis of two trials involving 979 participants, where SFA intake was reduced to less than 9% of total energy, also showed no clear effects on these outcomes. The evidence, graded using the GRADE framework, was assessed as low certainty for these outcomes. Trials were included in the less than 10% group if the intervention group achieved SFA intake below 10% of total energy, while the control group consumed more than 10%. This group also encompassed trials from the less than 9%, less than 8%, and less than 7% groups. A summary of results from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and observational studies comparing SFA intake below 10% versus above 10% showed an 8% reduction in all-cause mortality risk and a 9% reduction in cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk, though the latter was not statistically significant. No associations were observed for other outcomes. Analysis of blood lipid profiles indicated that reducing SFA intake consistently lowered low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol across the range of SFA intakes studied, suggesting benefits in reducing SFA intake to below 10% of total energy. The overall certainty of evidence for the effects of consuming less than 10% SFA compared to more than 10% on adult outcomes was assessed as low. For children, the certainty of evidence was high, based on extrapolation from adult data without downgrading for indirectness. Subgroup analysis revealed that replacing SFA with polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) reduced CVD risk by 21% and coronary heart disease (CHD) risk by 24%, though the latter was not statistically significant. Replacing SFA with monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs), carbohydrates, or protein showed no significant effects on cardiovascular or mortality outcomes, except for one small trial using olive oil as an intervention. Replacing SFA with PUFAs was associated with a 15% reduction in all-cause mortality risk, a 10% reduction in CVD risk, and an 11% reduction in CHD risk, though the CVD association was not statistically significant. Replacing SFA with plant-based MUFAs was associated with a 15% reduction in all-cause mortality risk, a 10% reduction in CVD risk, and a 17% reduction in CHD risk, though the CHD association was not statistically significant. No associations were observed for replacing SFA with animal-based MUFAs. Replacing SFA with carbohydrates from unspecified sources was associated with an 8% reduction in all-cause mortality risk, while replacing SFA with whole grains or low glycemic index foods reduced CHD risk by 6%. Conversely, replacing SFA with free sugars or high glycemic index foods increased CHD risk by 8%, though this was not statistically significant. Replacing SFA with protein from unspecified or animal sources was associated with a 26% and 31% increase in CHD risk, respectively. No association was observed for replacing SFA with plant-based protein. The certainty of evidence for replacing SFA with various macronutrients was assessed as moderate for plant-based MUFAs, low for PUFAs, unspecified MUFAs, whole grains, low glycemic index foods, and animal-based protein, and very low for free sugars, high glycemic index foods, and unspecified protein. For trans-fatty acids (TFAs), systematic reviews found that reducing TFA intake was associated with a 10% reduction in all-cause mortality risk, a 12% reduction in CVD risk, and a 14% reduction in CHD risk. Limited data were available for industrially produced versus ruminant TFAs, but industrially produced TFAs were associated with a 22% reduction in CHD risk when intake was lower. Reducing TFA intake improved blood lipid profiles, including reductions in LDL cholesterol. The certainty of evidence for the effects of lower TFA intake on critical outcomes was assessed as moderate. Replacing TFAs with PUFAs was associated with a 28% reduction in type 2 diabetes risk. Replacing TFAs with plant-based MUFAs was associated with a 10% reduction in all-cause mortality risk and a 20% reduction in CHD risk. No associations were observed for replacing TFAs with animal-based MUFAs. Replacing TFAs with carbohydrates from unspecified sources showed no significant associations.
